item.title: Writing Is Not a Checkpoint: Teaching Contextual Judgment in the AI Era
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

At the public library desk, questions about writing often arrive as requests for technical help. Patrons drafting personal statements need to decide which details about their experience to include; people completing online forms need to interpret questions before answering them. Helping patrons make writing decisions has been as much a part of my library work as explaining where to click.

I encounter similar questions in online writing courses. Students bring rules such as “never use I,” “always write five paragraphs,” and “never use artificial intelligence.” Some rules are assignment requirements; others are writing conventions students have learned to apply everywhere. Contextual judgment requires understanding what a rule accomplishes and when it applies. Students need opportunities to explain their choices within course requirements and ask for clarification when an expectation is unclear.

Rhetoric and composition scholar Sharon Crowley described required freshman English as a “border checkpoint,” where students had to establish their right to belong in higher education (1991, 160). She argued for ending the universal requirement while retaining the course as an elective (170). I draw on her account of gatekeeping to ask a narrower classroom question: How can instructors teach judgment while assessing compliance with assignment requirements? AI policies establish what is permitted; instruction must help students judge whether a permitted use serves the assignment’s purpose. The following examples illustrate ways to teach contextual judgment through activities and feedback you can adapt to your own courses.

Start with the Rules Students Bring

Nancy Walker, who helped me learn to teach writing, was an English professor and director of freshman English at what was then Southwest Missouri State University. In her 1987 statement, “Thoughts About Teaching,” she described how students could move from rigid right-or-wrong thinking to the belief that every judgment was a matter of personal preference. She called for “contextual deciding,” in which students evaluate ideas in context, commit to a choice, and remain willing to reconsider it (2).

A writing rules inventory offers one way to practice contextual deciding. Early in the course, ask students to list three rules they have learned. Have them choose one and explain where they learned it, what purpose it might serve, and when it might be useful. Follow the inventory with examples that test the rule’s limits.

To test “never use I,” compare two sentences. “I interviewed three residents” identifies who gathered the evidence. If a writer has verified a survey’s respondent count, adding “I believe” to “The survey had 40 respondents” makes the count sound uncertain. In this example, the qualification is unnecessary; the first-person pronoun is not the problem. Ask students to explain the difference, revise the rule, and test it on a sentence from a draft. Discuss how the revised rule accounts for the writer’s purpose.

Make Transfer Explicit

Walker urged teachers to plan activities that make discovery possible (1987, 1–2). Students who have already written a research paper may need help identifying what a new research task asks them to do differently.

The Elon Statement on Writing Transfer emphasizes reflection on how writers adapt prior learning to new tasks (Center for Engaged Learning 2015). For a memo recommending a course of action to a busy supervisor, ask students to write a brief transfer note before they draft the memo. Which practices from an earlier research essay can they reuse? What will they need to change for this reader and purpose?

Ask students to identify one adjustment, such as placing a recommendation before its supporting explanation. After students draft the memo, have them revisit the note and explain how a specific passage addresses the supervisor’s needs. Compare the passage with the explanation and give feedback on any needed revision. Students can consult the note when deciding whether the same strategy fits a later assignment.

Use the Problem as Material

Walker described a student who was stuck writing about his father. She helped him notice that his draft expressed affection as well as criticism (1987, 3–4). When students hesitate over an AI revision, ask them to compare the original and suggested wording and explain how the change affects the claim. The Association for Writing Across the Curriculum recommends reflection on whether and how AI serves a writing task (AWAC Working Group on AI in WAC 2025).

Explain permitted uses of AI before students begin an assignment. A process note does not authorize prohibited assistance. After major assignments in my online writing courses, I ask for an AI Use Note or process note that acknowledges assistance and examines the writer’s decisions:

- What tools or other assistance did you use, and for which parts of the assignment?

- Which suggestions did you accept, change, or reject, and why?

- How did you check the claims and sources you used?

- What alternatives did you consider for one writing decision, and why did you choose your approach?

Students who worked without AI can describe research and revision decisions. For students who used AI, the note should address how they evaluated AI suggestions and whether their use met the assignment’s rules. Instructors can collect the note with a draft and give feedback students can use during revision.

If students cite a source without reading it, ask them to read it and check whether it supports the claim. Have students correct any unsupported claim or inaccurate citation. Read the note alongside the draft to discuss whether the explanation matches the writing. A plausible explanation alone does not establish authorship or compliance.…

item.title: Is Your Class Worth It?: Connecting Classes to Workforce Skills
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear structure, useful vocabulary

It’s no secret that college tuition is rising rapidly causing students to rethink the value of a college degree and consider alternative paths to a career. How will your class help them meet their career goals and improve their job skills? Addressing those questions in course planning and design can yield impressive results including increased focus and motivation, a positive effect on students’ approach to assignments, and changing viewpoints on homework assignments as valuable learning experiences.

These outcomes can be achieved with three simple steps: a first day discussion, homework that asks students to read about classroom skills in action and reflect on how they will use the same skills in their careers, and TILTed (Transparency in Learning and Teaching) assignments that show students the purpose for homework and/or major assignments.

1. The First Day Discussion

Instead of starting class with introductions or discussing the syllabus, start by asking students how they think your class will help them. In my freshman English classes I ask, “Why do you think NSU requires this class? Why do you think it might be important?” Prompt them to brainstorm why the class is part of their degree program. What skills will they learn that will help them in other classes, their lives, and careers? Write the answers on the board or type them and project them onto a screen. Put added emphasis on career skills learned and give examples of how they will be used.

For example, in my English course I might mention using narrative writing skills when preparing an accident report for a police officer or a client progress report for a physical therapist or using argument essay skills to write a proposal for new equipment at work.

2. Homework About Skills In Action

Use interviews or case studies of the skills in action in the workplace for each unit. In my English 1010 course I have students read an interview with a working professional discussing narrative writing, evaluations, and argument essay skills and how they use them on the job. Once students read the interviews, I ask them to write one or two paragraphs discussing how they will use this skill or skills in their daily lives, in classes, and/or in their future careers.

Good interviews are provided in The McGraw Hill Guide, 5th edition and Business Communication Today, 16th edition. Interviews are also available online or a guest speaker could be invited to the class.

If you only have time to make one change, this one generated the most positive feedback on student surveys.

3. TILTed (Transparency in Learning and Teaching) Assignments

TILTed assignments are constructed around a Purpose, Task, and Criteria. I reworked each major assignment in my freshman English classes to meet the TILTed framework for Spring 2026, focusing especially on the purpose section. This strongly connects the writing task with the reasons for doing it such as meeting objectives of the class and future workforce duties.

For example, for a narrative writing assignment, the purpose was as follows: “This assignment eases you into the types of academic writing expected in a college setting while also letting you express yourself creatively by writing your own story. It helps you meet the goals and objectives of the class by demonstrating writing as a purpose-driven process of communication and demonstrating writing to diverse audiences, for a specific purpose, in a specific context. It also enhances skills needed for the workplace where narrative is part of many different writing tasks such as writing an incident report for a police officer, writing a patient progress report for a physical therapist, or writing a pupil progress report as a teacher.

More information about TILTed assignments is available at https://www.tilthighered.com/resources or https://www.uwidocs.org/2020/03/31/tilt-your-assignment-prompts/.

Results—What Did Students Think?

Throughout the Spring 2026 semester, through talking to students and grading homework submissions, I knew the new framework was helpful, but I also gathered data for the TILTed versus unTILTed assignments in my online literature course and the overall framework using all three moves in my freshman English courses. Students were given a Microsoft Forms survey to complete with extra credit points given for participation.

When rating the workforce skills homework assignments where they read an interview with a working professional discussing using the learned skills and then reflected on how they would use them in their own lives, 81% of the students said the homework helped them see the essays “as a valuable learning experience rather than just ‘busy’ work.”

Further, 95% of students said the homework assignments helped them to understand the relevance of each essay type for their future careers.

Ranking from 1 to 5, with 5 being the highest level, students ranked reflecting on the practical applications of these essay types as affecting their focus and motivation while writing the essays at a 4.24 level overall. Since focus and motivation are often lacking in English courses, I was happy to see such positive results in this area.

Students were also asked “if the homework assignments about workplace skills helped you improve focus and motivation when writing the essays, explain how and why.”

Among the more positive comments were, “[It] helped me see a point to the writing,” “It allowed me to put in perspective how important it is to learn how to write correctly and how I will use this in my future career,” and “When doing these homeworks they were not just busy work they were a way to help reflect on what we would be doing and how we should go about writing these essays in an appropriate way.”…
